contests.office_does: One of nine statewide-elected justices on Washington's court of last resort, deciding appeals, state constitutional questions, and the rules that govern every court in the state.
contests.race_blurb: A race for the two years left on retired Justice Mary Yu's term. Justice Colleen Melody, appointed by Governor Ferguson and on the court since January 2026, led the August primary with 53% against tax and constitutional attorney Scott Edwards (29%), who runs on applying the law "as written" and against the appointment pipeline.

candidates.summary: Sitting justice since January 2026, appointed after leading the Attorney General's Civil Rights Division. She calls state law "the backbone of a lot of our rights right now" and is endorsed by every sitting justice.
highlights: On the Supreme Court since January 2026; wrote the 5-4 majority in In re Marriage of Hauk (Child Relocation Act) and joined the 6-3 majority striking the natural-gas initiative [S6][S8]
Says "State law is really the backbone of a lot of our rights right now" and names Justice Kagan as a model for attention to rulings' practical effects [S9][S10]
Also told the Seattle Times the court should "stay in its lane, and not veer into policy, unnecessarily" [S12]
Led the AG's Civil Rights Division, including the travel-ban challenge [S18]
Endorsed by all sitting justices, Governors Ferguson, Inslee and Gregoire, and the State Labor Council; first in the primary with 53.03% [S1][S14]

judicial.basis: Repeatedly frames state law and state courts as rights guarantors and cites practical effects (Kagan model); her 'stay in its lane' remark and text-based Hauk opinion keep her off the pole. Down from +2 in the primary because the refreshed record adds those moderating items.

experience.basis: Incumbent with the full institutional roster behind her, but appointed and on the bench only since January 2026 after a government litigation career; evidence unchanged in substance from the primary.

candidates.summary: Bainbridge Island tax and constitutional attorney with 30-plus years of practice, including more than a dozen Washington Supreme Court cases, and no judicial service. He runs on applying the constitution and laws "as written" and on electing rather than appointing justices.
highlights: Pamphlet: "The role of the Supreme Court is to apply the constitution and laws as written, not rewrite them" [S1]
Says the court's century-old ruling against a progressive income tax "got it right"; has litigated against the capital gains and Seattle payroll taxes [S6][S8]
Says he wished the dissent in the natural-gas initiative case had been the majority [S5]
No judicial service; says justices "should be responsible to the people, not to the governor" [S2][S7]
Recommended by the state Republican Party; second in the primary with 29.46% [S6][S9]

judicial.basis: Repeated explicit as-written statements across the pamphlet, a June Q&A ('You cannot inject your policy views') and October interviews; evidence strengthened since the primary, score unchanged.

experience.basis: Never held judicial office and runs against the appointment pipeline, but offers a 30-year litigation record rather than a pure renewal case; unchanged from the primary.

contests.office_does: One of nine statewide-elected justices on Washington's court of last resort, deciding appeals, state constitutional questions, and the rules that govern every court in the state.
contests.race_blurb: An open seat. Mason County Superior Court Judge David Stevens, a self-described textualist and originalist and critic of the court's criminal-procedure rules, finished first in the August primary (35.3%) against King County Superior Court Judge Jaime Hawk (33.4%), a former public defender and ACLU attorney backed by most sitting justices and the governor.

candidates.summary: Mason County Superior Court judge, elected in 2023 over an appointed incumbent, with a career spanning state, federal and international prosecution and public defense. He describes himself as a textualist and originalist and criticizes recent Supreme Court rules on criminal procedure.
highlights: Site: the state constitution "should be interpreted based on its text and original meaning and not on evolving societal standards" [S3]
Criticizes the court's juvenile-warrant, arraignment-deadline and jury-selection rules and supports failure-to-appear warrants [S3][S10]
About a decade as a Spokane County deputy prosecutor, plus federal prosecutor and public-defender roles [S1][S8]
Argues appointment of judges "leads to ideological and political decisions"; reached the bench by defeating an appointed incumbent [S1][S4][S8]
First in the primary with 35.29%; endorsed by WACOPS and recommended by the state Republican Party [S7][S8]

judicial.basis: Self-described textualist/originalist; text-and-original-meaning reading of the constitution and 'not for the courts to lead the way'; unchanged from the primary, now with more statements.

safety.basis: Documented positions against the court's juvenile-warrant, arraignment-deadline and bail-related rule changes and for failure-to-appear warrants, on a prosecution-heavy career; public-defender years keep it off -2. Confidence raised from medium because the positions are now repeated across his site and news interviews.

experience.basis: A sitting elected trial judge who campaigns as the outsider to the appointment pipeline; unchanged from the primary.

candidates.summary: King County Superior Court judge since a 2022 appointment, formerly a state and federal public defender and ACLU of Washington attorney. She describes a text-first approach and focuses on court funding, juror pay and access to lawyers.
highlights: Says her approach starts from the text, then legislative intent where the text is ambiguous [S9]
Says overturning precedent must meet the "incorrect ... and harmful" threshold, citing recent reversals tied to racial-justice concerns as examples [S10]
Former juvenile and federal public defender and Legal Strategy Director for the ACLU-WA Smart Justice campaign [S3][S9]
Endorsed by Governor Ferguson, Chief Justice Stephens and several justices, and the State Labor Council [S1][S4]
Second in the primary with 33.37%; leads in campaign fundraising (about $310,600 to about $62,200) [S6][S8][S9]

judicial.basis: Text-first method, but her precedent answer holds up recent reversals of 'harmful and incorrect' precedent tied to racial justice as legitimate examples, and The Urbanist endorsed her as a 'reformer'. Raised from the primary's refutation-adjusted 0 on this new forum evidence; medium because it rests on one forum answer plus an endorser's characterization.

safety.basis: Professional formation is defense and civil liberties (juvenile and federal public defender, ACLU-WA Smart Justice); no documented bail or diversion statements, so not +2. Evidence unchanged from the primary.

experience.basis: Sitting trial judge since a 2022 gubernatorial appointment, backed by the governor and most sitting justices; unchanged from the primary.

contests.office_does: One of nine statewide-elected justices on Washington's court of last resort, deciding appeals, state constitutional questions, and the rules that govern every court in the state.
contests.race_blurb: An open seat: Justice Charles W. Johnson must retire at 75, and only two candidates filed, so the race skipped the primary. Court of Appeals Judge Ian Birk, backed by most sitting justices and labor, faces King County Superior Court Judge Sean O'Donnell, a former prosecutor backed by the Seattle Times, law enforcement, the state Republican Party and Democratic officials including Gregoire; O'Donnell's Republican recommendation and Birk's fundraising emails about it have become a point of dispute.

candidates.summary: Division I Court of Appeals judge since a 2022 appointment, after 20 years as a civil litigator representing consumers and policyholders. He points to 200-plus appellate opinions and the backing of most sitting justices.
highlights: Court of Appeals judge since April 2022 (appointed, then retained unopposed), with more than 200 authored opinions [S6][S3]
Wrote the published opinion letting the Attorney General subpoena Archdiocese of Seattle records on clergy abuse, within religion-clause limits [S8]
Says the state constitution is "more important now than it ever has" been and that he decides cases with "respect for legal precedent" [S11][S5]
Endorsed by seven sitting justices, AG Brown, the State Labor Council and King County Democrats; rated Exceptionally Well Qualified by Washington Women Lawyers [S4][S11][S1][S17]
His campaign's emails calling O'Donnell "a Republican-affiliated judge" drew a letter from 62 judges and a Seattle Times editorial [S14][S15]

experience.basis: Sitting appellate judge with institutional support from most of the court, but four years on the bench by appointment; new candidate, first scoring.

safety.basis: In his own written questionnaire answers he reports taking a National Judicial College seminar on 'reducing disparity through nontraditional diversion' and says he intends to bring that to his work, alongside a call for judges to address the system's 'disproportionate impact on communities of color and people of limited means' [S7]. This is a single clear first-person statement favoring diversion, which the judicial safety rule accepts. Not higher, because he has no criminal-law formation and no bail or diversion rulings.

candidates.summary: King County Superior Court judge since 2013 and former 12-year King County prosecutor, including the Green River Task Force. He emphasizes trial-court leadership and victims' voices and has a cross-partisan endorsement list.
highlights: Superior Court judge since 2013; former Chief Criminal and Chief Unified Family Court judge and Superior Court Judges' Association president [S6][S3]
Prosecutor 2001-2013, including the Green River Task Force and the state's first human trafficking case [S1][S6]
Says judges can "honor victims' rights while vigorously protecting defendants' constitutional guarantees"; helped start a protection-order court [S4][S1]
Rated Exceptionally Well Qualified by the King County Bar Association; endorsed by the Seattle Times, Gregoire, Reps. Smith and Strickland, and law enforcement [S14][S1][S7]
The state Republican Party recommends him; he declined to disavow it, citing judicial-conduct limits [S10][S11]

safety.basis: Twelve-year prosecution formation and a campaign centered on victims' voices and firearm surrender; his campaign-reported pretrial-release reform work keeps it off -2. No documented bail or diversion rulings.

experience.basis: Nearly 14 years as a trial judge with chief-judge and statewide association leadership, running on that record; new candidate, first scoring.

contests.office_does: One of nine statewide-elected justices on Washington's court of last resort, deciding appeals, state constitutional questions, and the rules that govern every court in the state.
contests.race_blurb: A race for the two years left on retired Justice Barbara Madsen's term. Justice Theo Angelis, appointed by Governor Ferguson in April 2026, led the August primary (35.9%) over retired Federal Way Municipal Court Judge Dave Larson (32.2%), who runs on trial-bench experience, applying the law "as written" and changing how justices are appointed.

candidates.summary: Sitting justice appointed by Governor Ferguson in 2026 after 26 years at K&L Gates, where he led the appellate and IP practices, with pro bono immigration work. He has no authored opinions yet and the backing of all his colleagues.
highlights: On the Supreme Court since April 4, 2026; no authored opinions found through October 1, 2026 [S3][S4]
Says the court's role is to "apply the law fairly, independently, neutrally, and consistently" and that he has ruled against his own view when the law required it [S10][S9]
26 years at K&L Gates; pro bono litigation over children without lawyers in immigration court [S1][S3]
Endorsed by the Seattle Times for the general, all of his colleagues, and Governors Ferguson and Gregoire; rated Exceptionally Well Qualified by two bar groups [S11][S1][S13][S14]
First in the primary with 35.92% [S16]

experience.basis: Runs as the incumbent with the court's and governors' institutional backing, but six months on the bench by appointment; evidence unchanged in substance from the primary.

candidates.summary: Retired Federal Way Municipal Court presiding judge with 18 years on the bench and 23 as a trial lawyer, and a repeat Supreme Court candidate who lost the 2024 race by about 20,000 votes. He runs as a critic of the court's direction and the appointment process.
highlights: Site: "Apply the law as written, not as you wish it had been" [S4]
Called the Blake decision "motivated by ideology" and opposed proposed bail rules he said would "cripple" trial courts [S2]
Served on the DMCJA Therapeutic Courts Committee 2019-2025 [S6]
Proposes a bipartisan Judicial Elections Commission to vet appointees [S8][S9]
Second in the primary with 32.24%; the one located 2026 bar rating is "Qualified" (Tacoma-Pierce County Bar) [S16][S11]

judicial.basis: New campaign-site statement 'Apply the law as written, not as you wish it had been' and 'not to impose ideology', on top of the primary's Blake-was-ideological criticism. Moved from -1 to -2; medium because it rests on campaign-site wording plus one earlier interview.

safety.basis: Genuinely mixed: opposed proposed bail rules and says court decisions weakened trial courts' response to crime, yet served six years on the Therapeutic Courts Committee and campaigns on 'compassion and accountability'; unchanged from the primary.

experience.basis: Long judicial tenure (18 years, municipal level) but campaigns as an outsider against the appointed incumbent and the appointment process; unchanged from the primary.

contests.office_does: One of nine statewide-elected justices on Washington's court of last resort, deciding appeals, state constitutional questions, and the rules that govern every court in the state.
contests.race_blurb: Chief Justice Debra Stephens, on the court since 2008, led the August primary with 54.5% against Tacoma tax attorney and Navy veteran Todd Bloom (27.2%), who has never held judicial office and criticizes the court's McCleary, Quinn and natural-gas initiative rulings.

candidates.summary: Chief Justice and a justice since 2008, formerly a Court of Appeals judge and Gonzaga appellate lawyer and professor. She describes a text-and-structure method applied to a constitution written as a broad framework, and wrote McCleary.
highlights: On the court since 2008, Chief Justice since January 2025 [S1][S7]
Wrote McCleary (2012), recognizing a positive constitutional right to amply funded K-12 education [S2][S6]
Wrote the 6-3 majority striking Initiative 2066 on single-subject grounds [S4][S10]
Describes "respect for text and structure" and admires Justice Brennan's view that "rights without remedies are hollow" [S9]
Endorsed by all other sitting justices and 150+ judges; first in the primary with 54.50% [S3][S7]

judicial.basis: Constitution as a broad framework applied with fidelity to purposes, broader state protections, Brennan's 'rights without remedies are hollow', and authorship of McCleary; her stated respect for text and structure keeps it at +1. Unchanged from the primary.

experience.basis: Eighteen years on the court, current Chief Justice, prior Court of Appeals service and the whole court's endorsement; unchanged from the primary.

candidates.summary: Tacoma tax and business attorney, CPA and Navy veteran who serves on the WSBA Board of Governors and has never held judicial office. He runs on judicial restraint and criticizes several of the court's major rulings.
highlights: Says judges should "faithfully apply the law as written" and exercise "judicial restraint" [S3][S10]
Says Quinn was "wrongly decided" and the McCleary contempt sanctions overstepped the separation of powers [S4][S7]
Also says judges must consider how rulings are received and give more weight to voter-approved measures [S7]
No judicial service; FINRA arbitrator 1999-2020 and active-duty Navy officer 2002-2013 [S1]
Recommended by the state Republican Party; second in the primary with 27.20% [S5][S8]

judicial.basis: Repeated restraint and as-written statements and criticism of McCleary and Quinn; medium, not high, because he also says judges must weigh how rulings will be received. Unchanged from the primary.

experience.basis: No judicial service and frames the race as a choice to 'give someone new your vote'; unchanged from the primary.

contests.office_does: The King County Assessor sets the property values that county property taxes are based on, keeps parcel records and runs exemption programs; the office does not set tax rates or levies.
contests.race_blurb: Open seat. City of Seattle appraiser Rob Foxcurran led the August primary with 47%; property-rights advocate Dominique Scarimbolo edged Shoreline Councilmember Christopher Roberts for second with 19%.

candidates.summary: City of Seattle Senior Appraiser and former King County Board of Appeals and Equalization hearing examiner, running for his first elected office on accuracy, transparency and property-tax relief.
highlights: Senior Appraiser for the City of Seattle and Certified General Real Estate Appraiser; formerly a hearing examiner on the county Board of Appeals and Equalization [S1]
Would push the Legislature for a homestead exemption and a renter's tax credit, and wants property taxes tied to income [S1][S3]
Says large corporate landowners use appeals experts to shift the tax burden onto homeowners and renters [S1][S3]
Would use the office's data to identify surplus public land for affordable housing [S3]
Endorsed by King County Democrats, Executive Zahilay, primary opponent Al Dams and the Seattle Times, Stranger and Urbanist (primary) [S1][S9][S10]

taxes.basis: Wants corporations to pay their fair share and property taxes tied to income, and called for lifting the 1% levy cap in his primary statement; pairs this with targeted homeowner and renter relief rather than lower overall collections.

housing.basis: Proposes using the Assessor's data to identify surplus public land for affordable housing and a state renter's tax credit.

experience.basis: No elected office, but a professional record in the office's core work (appraisal, assessment appeals) and the backing of the county party, labor and the office's own chief deputy.

candidates.summary: Small family business owner and King County chapter president of the Citizens Alliance for Property Rights, running as a taxpayer advocate who is "not a politician."
highlights: President of the King County chapter of the Citizens Alliance for Property Rights; small business owner [S1]
Calls for parcel-specific valuation breakdowns, timely appeals and due process for property owners [S1]
Submitted four audit requests to the County Auditor on assessment uniformity, valuation methods, levy stacking and appeals [S3]
Told KUOW she opposes property taxes and that residents are "overtaxed" [S6]
Rated "Best Choice" by the King County Republican Party; raised about $250 as of August [S6][S7]

taxes.basis: Told KUOW she opposes property taxes and residents are overtaxed; campaigns on keeping people from being taxed out of their homes and asked for an audit of levy lid lifts as a workaround to the 1% limit.

spending.basis: Platform centers on audits, open-books government and demanding fiscal responsibility, and she attributes funding gaps to waste and fraud.

experience.basis: Runs explicitly as "not a politician" with no elected or assessment-office experience, offering a taxpayer and appellant's perspective.

contests.office_does: A U.S. Representative writes and votes on federal law, including taxes and appropriations, oversees the executive branch, and handles constituent casework for the district.
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Suzan DelBene (D), in office since 2012 and chair of House Democrats' campaign committee, faces Republican Mary Silva, an Everett audiologist making her first run beyond party precinct posts. DelBene led the primary with 53% to Silva's 26%.

candidates.summary: U.S. Representative since 2012 on the Ways and Means Committee and 2026 chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee; former Microsoft executive and state Revenue director.
highlights: Campaigns on lowering costs, a permanent expanded Child Tax Credit and having "the wealthy pay their fair share" [S1]
Introduced the CHEATERS Act in July 2026 to restore $83 billion in IRS funding aimed at high-income tax evasion [S6]
Wants to roll back Medicaid cuts, lower premiums and "rein in out-of-control ICE agents" [S1]
Supports reproductive rights and opposes a nationwide abortion ban; voted against H.R. 28 on girls' sports in 2025 [S1][S15]
Said in July that "Americans should not be subsidizing" the Netanyahu government's conduct, while voting against the Massie amendment that would have cut aid [S7][S9]

taxes.basis: Says the wealthy must pay their fair share and sponsored the CHEATERS Act on high-income tax enforcement, while also seeking tax cuts for working families rather than new progressive taxes.

spending.basis: Platform expands programs (permanent monthly Child Tax Credit, reversing Medicaid and food-assistance cuts, two million affordable homes) without an audit-first theme.

climate.basis: Criticizes cuts to green-energy investment, sponsored the carbon-based Clean Competition Act, and voted against rolling back EPA approvals of California emission rules.

experience.basis: Fourteen years in the House on Ways and Means with an enacted bill, plus prior service as state Revenue director.

reform.basis: Chairs the DCCC, her party's national House campaign operation, and raised about $1.48 million of $3.55 million from political committees.

immigration.basis: Calls for immigration reform and reining in "out-of-control ICE agents" in her pamphlet; no sponsored immigration bills recorded in the dossier.

healthcare.basis: Health agenda works within the current system: lower premiums, restore Medicaid, strengthen Medicare, and oversight of Medicare's AI claims-review program; no single-payer position.

social.basis: States strong support for reproductive rights and opposition to a national abortion ban, and voted against H.R. 28 restricting girls' sports by sex.

tech.basis: Repeated sponsor of the Email Privacy Act and other digital-privacy bills; seeking disclosure on AI-driven Medicare claim reviews.

defense.basis: Says the U.S. should not subsidize the Netanyahu government's conduct and voted against the anti-boycott bill and FY2027 NDAA, but voted against the Massie amendment cutting aid.

candidates.summary: Everett clinical audiologist and Republican precinct committee officer making her first run for public office.
highlights: Pamphlet focuses on reshoring manufacturing, cybersecurity of grids and data, and help for small and medium-sized businesses [S1]
Platform calls for a full Pentagon audit, an overhaul of intelligence-agency contracting and a new 9/11 investigation [S4]
Would end warrantless mass surveillance, including Flock license-plate cameras, and require warrants for location data [S4]
Supports voter ID and a midweek national voting holiday [S4]
Raised $8,434 through September, including $5,629 of her own money [S10]

taxes.basis: Wants small-business tax incentives and a lower overall burden, but also targets offshore tax havens and "corporate welfare" that she says costs trillions in lost revenue.

spending.basis: Platform centers on auditing the Pentagon, curbing intelligence-contractor spending and cracking down on misuse of taxpayer funds, while also proposing new federal cybersecurity investment.

climate.basis: Told the Herald she is "not a big believer in the climate change narrative"; no specific energy or carbon policy.

experience.basis: Has never held public office; prior roles are clinical, managerial and party precinct posts.

immigration.basis: Platform says "Fortify border security" and calls for restructuring H-1B visas toward local hiring; told the Herald she favors controlled immigration and opposes open borders.

tech.basis: Would dismantle warrantless surveillance, require warrants for location and video data, and impose cybersecurity requirements on federal contractors.

defense.basis: Calls for a comprehensive Pentagon audit and curbs on military-contractor payouts; her site hosts a video titled "How Does Netanyahu Get Away With War Crimes?"

contests.office_does: A U.S. Representative writes and votes on federal legislation, controls federal spending through appropriations, oversees the executive branch, and provides constituent services for the district.
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Pramila Jayapal (D), in the House since 2017, faces Republican Nirav Sheth, a Marine veteran and former police officer making his second run for Congress. Jayapal took 84% of the primary vote to Sheth's 10%.

candidates.summary: Incumbent U.S. Representative since 2017 and former state senator; Chair Emerita of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and ranking member of the House Immigration Subcommittee.
highlights: Leads the Medicare for All Act and backs an ultra-millionaire wealth tax [S1]
Authored the Iran War Powers resolution that passed the House 214-208 in July 2026; voted against the FY2027 NDAA [S5][S6]
Released a National AI Charter Act framework in October 2026 requiring AI companies to hold a federal charter [S8]
Co-chairs the Trans Equality Task Force; endorsed by Planned Parenthood, the State Labor Council and Fuse Washington [S1][S11]
Raised about $2.5 million through the pre-primary report [S3]

taxes.basis: Pamphlet backs an ultra-millionaire wealth tax; sponsored the Ultra-Millionaire Tax Act of 2026 (H.R. 8085).

spending.basis: Leads bills to expand federal programs: Medicare for All, tuition-free college, housing as a human right.

safety.basis: Sponsored the Housing not Handcuffs Act and a moratorium on government facial-recognition use, pointing toward non-enforcement responses.

climate.basis: Pamphlet says she works to fight climate change and is Sierra Club-endorsed; no specific 2026 climate bill recorded.

experience.basis: Ten years in the House with subcommittee ranking-member and caucus leadership roles.

reform.basis: Says she never takes corporate PAC money and leads a congressional stock-trading ban and Supreme Court reform; FEC shows $280,500 from other political committees, so not a full pole_b case.

immigration.basis: Campaigns against 'lawless ICE and CBP actions,' sponsored the ICE Out of Our Faces and Dignity for Detained Immigrants Acts, and opposes rescissions targeting immigration services.

healthcare.basis: Leads the Medicare for All Act, framing universal healthcare as a right.

social.basis: Co-chairs the Trans Equality Task Force, sponsored a Transgender Bill of Rights resolution, and campaigns on protecting abortion rights.

tech.basis: National AI Charter Act framework (federal charters, pre-release testing, kill switch, strict liability) and a biometric-surveillance moratorium.

defense.basis: Voted against the FY2027 NDAA, for the Massie amendment to cut Israel military aid, and authored the Iran War Powers resolution.

candidates.summary: Republican candidate who has not held elected office; Marine veteran and former Lakewood police officer who is CFO of a Meineke franchise group and co-owned a restaurant from 2018 to 2025.
highlights: Campaigns on 'bringing law & order back to Seattle,' police hiring and mandatory treatment for repeat drug offenders [S1][S4]
Opposes Washington's new income tax, the Climate Commitment Act and other state taxes [S6]
Supports the girls' sports initiative and a biological definition of sex under Title IX [S5]
Immigrant from India who backs border security alongside streamlined legal immigration [S3][S7]
Raised about $11,800 through the pre-primary report [S8]

taxes.basis: Campaign site opposes the state income tax, the millionaires tax, the CCA, the services sales tax, the estate tax and lifting the property-tax cap.

spending.basis: Promises 'military-grade accountability' over tax dollars and an audit of the CCA, while also backing infrastructure and police funding.

safety.basis: Law-and-order platform: hire more police, mandatory treatment for repeat drug offenders, let cities refuse supportive housing linked to crime; the pamphlet also states a housing goal for homelessness.

climate.basis: Calls the Climate Commitment Act 'a hidden tax' raising fuel and utility costs and stresses energy independence; proposes auditing rather than repealing the CCA.

experience.basis: No elected office; Marine, police and small-business background.

immigration.basis: Pairs border security and cooperation on removing violent offenders with streamlining legal immigration.

social.basis: Supports the 'Protecting Fairness in Girls' Sports' initiative and a biological definition of sex under Title IX; no abortion position found.

tech.basis: Wants to 'restore a business environment that supports technology including AI innovation.'

contests.office_does: A U.S. Representative writes and votes on federal law, including taxes and appropriations, oversees the executive branch, and handles constituent casework and district project funding.
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Kim Schrier (D), a pediatrician first elected in 2018, faces Republican Spencer Meline, a Leavenworth restaurant owner in his first campaign, in a district that spans eastern King County and both sides of the Cascades. Schrier took 53% in the primary to Meline's 16%.

candidates.summary: U.S. Representative since 2019 and former Issaquah pediatrician on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, seeking a fifth term.
highlights: Cites bills capping insulin costs and letting Medicare negotiate drug prices; wants Medicaid cuts and ACA premium credits reversed [S1][S3]
Introduced a bill to suspend the federal gas tax through year's end; her hydropower licensing bill became law in September 2026 [S1][S9]
Pro-choice; says she twice voted for the Women's Health Protection Act and voted against H.R. 28 on girls' sports [S4][S17]
Supports border security plus a path to citizenship and codifying DACA [S5]
Says she secured over $60 million in district projects, including body cameras and a rapid DNA system for King County law enforcement [S1]

taxes.basis: Proposes suspending the federal gas tax while criticizing Republican tax cuts for billionaires; no proposal for new progressive taxes.

spending.basis: Highlights $60 million in district projects and wants restored Medicaid and ACA credits plus more community health centers and school-based clinics.

safety.basis: Pledges to fight any effort to defund police and funded body cameras and a rapid DNA system for King County law enforcement, while also backing mental-health professionals alongside police.

climate.basis: Says climate change requires immediate action and voted against rolling back EPA approvals of California emission rules; also proposes a gas-tax suspension and backs hydropower and fusion.

experience.basis: Four terms in the House on Energy and Commerce, with a bill signed into law in 2026.

immigration.basis: Backs a path to citizenship and codifying DACA and says the administration is "terrorizing immigrant communities," while also calling for a secure border.

healthcare.basis: Health record and platform work within the existing system: insulin caps, Medicare drug negotiation, restoring Medicaid and ACA credits, community health centers; no single-payer position.

social.basis: Pro-choice and says she twice voted to codify Roe; voted against H.R. 28 restricting girls' sports by sex.

tech.basis: Says she led a bill to protect children's data from Big Tech and that "we need regulations to protect people and their data."

defense.basis: Voted for H.R. 4795 barring college boycotts of Israel (most Democrats opposed) and against the Massie amendment to cut aid; voted against the FY2027 NDAA.

candidates.summary: Leavenworth restaurant owner and first-time candidate endorsed by the state, King County and Snohomish County Republican parties.
highlights: Running on housing costs and small business; proposes first-time homebuyer tax relief, limits on institutional buyers of starter homes and a portable-mortgage pilot [S4][S6]
Supports congressional term limits, single-subject bills and a ban on members trading individual stocks [S4]
Calls for enforceable restraints on deficit growth and cuts to waste and unnecessary spending [S4]
Backs "all-of-the-above" energy including hydropower, nuclear, renewables, natural gas and domestic oil [S4]
Says "We shouldn't allow illegal entry at all" but is open to bipartisan reform of legal immigration [S5]

taxes.basis: Proposes tax incentives for small businesses, first-time homebuyer tax relief, capital-gains changes and tax-deductible premiums; no new taxes proposed.

spending.basis: Platform calls for enforceable restraints on deficit growth, cutting waste and unnecessary spending, and plain-English spending transparency.

climate.basis: All-of-the-above energy including natural gas and domestic oil to keep costs manageable, alongside hydropower, solar and fusion; no climate-policy commitments.

experience.basis: Never held office; runs as "not a politician" on small-business experience.

reform.basis: Platform backs congressional term limits, single-subject bills and a ban on individual stock trading by members; also runs with state and county party endorsements.

immigration.basis: Prioritizes border security and says illegal entry should not be allowed at all, while saying he is open to bipartisan reform of legal pathways.

tech.basis: Pairs "Government shouldn't try to stop innovation" and AI leadership goals with strong federal privacy law, antitrust enforcement against dominant tech firms and AI accountability.

contests.office_does: A U.S. Representative writes and votes on federal legislation, controls federal spending through appropriations, oversees the executive branch, and provides constituent services for the district.
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Adam Smith (D), in the House since 1997 and top Democrat on Armed Services, faces Republican Doug Basler for the sixth time. Smith took 47% and Basler 22% in a primary where two left-flank challengers split much of the remainder.

candidates.summary: Incumbent U.S. Representative since 1997, former state senator and Seattle prosecutor; ranking member and past chair of the House Armed Services Committee.
highlights: Voted against the FY2027 NDAA in July 2026, citing its $1.6 trillion price tag and anti-LGBTQ+ floor amendments [S6][S13]
Voted to block $3.3 billion in Israel military aid while saying he still supports Israel [S7][S14]
Introduced a resolution to tax capital gains the same as wages [S8]
Supports a path to single-payer healthcare and lists protecting abortion rights as a priority [S1][S3]

highlights: Pledges to pass SB 6358 to end corporate election spending in Washington [S1]
Calls for a progressive tax structure and universal health care [S2]
Will defend the Climate Commitment Act against raids on its funding [S1][S2]

taxes.basis: Calls for a progressive tax structure to end Washington's status as the second-most-regressive tax state.

housing.basis: Proposes state preemption to cut red tape on housing construction, a supply-side approach.

climate.basis: Pledges in his pamphlet and on his site to defend the Climate Commitment Act and modernize the grid.

experience.basis: First-time candidate with no elected experience, running against the House Minority Leader.

local-control.basis: Supports state preemption of local red tape on housing construction.

reform.basis: His signature issue is SB 6358, which would bar corporate, union, and nonprofit election spending.

healthcare.basis: Supports universal health care as 'more effective than the private insurance market.'

social.basis: Endorsed by Washington State Stonewall Democrats; no stated position on LGBTQ+ or reproductive policy.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital, and transportation budgets, serving a two-year term.
contests.race_blurb: An open seat between two Democrats: former Shoreline mayor Keith Scully and former FTC antitrust attorney Danica Noble, both dual-endorsed by the 32nd District Democrats and WEA-PAC.

candidates.summary: Shoreline councilmember and former mayor, attorney and former prosecutor, running on housing, climate, progressive tax reform paired with spending restraint, and limited AI regulation.
highlights: Calls the millionaires tax "the start, not the end" of tax reform and says Olympia needs to rein in spending [S3]
Would maintain the Climate Commitment Act and push toward 100% sustainable energy [S3]
Endorsed by the Seattle Times, The Stranger and Washington Conservation Action [S4]

taxes.basis: Supports the millionaires tax and progressive restructuring, but frames it as replacing regressive taxes rather than layering new ones and pairs it with spending restraint.

spending.basis: Says Olympia must rein in spending and earlier proposed a small across-the-board cut except education.

housing.basis: Mixes subsidies, tax credits and land trusts with streamlined permitting and support for state density mandates.

safety.basis: Cites bringing mental health professionals into the field in Shoreline; serves on the Regional Crisis Response Agency board.

climate.basis: Would maintain the Climate Commitment Act and push to 100% sustainable energy; former Futurewise legal director with conservation endorsements.

experience.basis: Ten years on the Shoreline council including as mayor, but no state legislative record.

immigration.basis: Supports banning masked law enforcement and defending state laws against federal overreach.

tech.basis: Favors limited, responsible AI regulation: disclosure, no AI in schools or with children, data centers only with clean energy.

local-control.basis: Says the state 'has taken important steps to mandate needed density' (state standards) and also wants 'more local freedom for districts to raise funds' (local control). Explicit statements point both ways.

candidates.summary: First-time candidate and former FTC antitrust attorney running on tech and AI guardrails, competition enforcement to lower prices, and school funding.
highlights: About 20 years at the FTC, including the antitrust case against Meta [S1][S4]
Would strengthen antitrust enforcement, ban surveillance pricing, and bar insurers from using AI to deny coverage [S3]
Endorsed by the Washington State Labor Council and Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates [S1][S6]

tech.basis: Campaign centers on guardrails for AI and tech targeting kids and workers, surveillance-pricing bans and limits on student data.

spending.basis: Calls for fully funding schools and investing in public hospitals while pledging to spend wisely with real accountability.

housing.basis: Pairs faster permitting and more supply at every income level with stronger renter protections.

experience.basis: First-time candidate offering federal enforcement expertise rather than an elected record.

healthcare.basis: Proposes stronger state insurance regulation and public-hospital investment within the existing system; no universal-coverage proposal.

immigration.basis: Opposes federal deportations of refugees and supports state help for refugees.

social.basis: Endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates; no statement of her own on reproductive or LGBTQ+ policy.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital, and transportation budgets, serving a two-year term.
contests.race_blurb: Democratic Rep. Edwin Obras, appointed in 2024 and elected in 2025, faces Republican newcomer Chris Martinez, who runs on lower taxes, repealing the Climate Commitment Act, and parental rights in schools.

candidates.summary: Incumbent since December 2024 and former Seattle Human Services division director, running on affordability, worker protections and immigrant rights.
highlights: Six bills signed in his first biennium, including background checks and rideshare regulation [S2]
Has pushed for rent-increase caps and voted for 2025 rent stabilization [S2][S7]
Voted for ESSB 6346 (2026 income tax over $1 million) and sponsored ESHB 1296 [S4][S6]

taxes.basis: Voted for the 2026 tax on income over $1 million; no campaign statements on taxes found.

spending.basis: Cites securing over $30 million in state investment for the district, including housing and health.

housing.basis: Pushes rent-increase caps and limits on investor home buying, and voted for rent stabilization.

experience.basis: Under two years in office but with six enacted bills and a whip post, against a political newcomer.

immigration.basis: Pamphlet pledges to keep fighting for immigrant rights, without specifics.

social.basis: Endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates; no statement of his own on reproductive or LGBTQ+ policy.

parental-rights.basis: Original sponsor of, and yes vote on, ESHB 1296, which amended the I-2081 parental-rights list.

candidates.summary: Republican precinct committee officer and blue-collar worker making his first run, on lower taxes, smaller government, repeal of the Climate Commitment Act and parental rights.
highlights: Lists "HB 6346 (Unconstitutional Income Tax)" among bills he opposes and wants lower B&O taxes [S2]
Would reduce or eliminate the Climate Commitment Act [S2]
Says parents have the right to know and guide what their children learn [S2]

taxes.basis: Opposes the new income tax, wants lower B&O taxes, and pledges to abolish energy taxes.

spending.basis: Would cut wasteful spending and reduce the size of state government.

housing.basis: Would cut regulations on home builders to make housing more affordable.

safety.basis: Runs on law and order, more officers, and holding criminals accountable.

climate.basis: Would reduce or eliminate the Climate Commitment Act and abolish energy taxes.

experience.basis: No elected office beyond appointed PCO; pitches himself as a blue-collar outsider.

parental-rights.basis: Says parents have the right to know and guide what children learn and opposes instruction without parental knowledge or consent.

social.basis: Campaigns on traditional family values; no specific statement on sports eligibility, gender-affirming care or abortion.

contests.office_does: One of 98 Washington State Representatives, serving two-year terms writing state law and the state budget for the 37th District (southeast Seattle, Skyway and part of Renton).
contests.race_blurb: House Education Committee chair Sharon Tomiko Santos, the state's longest-serving House member, trails first-time candidate Kelabe Tewolde after a 51.5% to 47.9% primary; both are Democrats. The sharpest policy split is rent stabilization, which Santos voted against and Tewolde supports.

candidates.summary: State Representative since 1999 and chair of the House Education Committee; voted for the 2026 millionaires' tax and against the 2025 rent-increase cap.
highlights: Only Seattle-area legislator to vote against the 2025 rent-increase cap, citing harm to small landlords [S6][S7][S8]
Voted for ESSB 6346, the millionaires' tax I-645 would repeal [S9]
As Education chair, signed the committee's do-pass report on HB 1296 (2025 parental-rights amendments) and voted for it on the floor [S10][S11]
Opposes a universal school cellphone ban, preferring local school-board decisions [S5]

taxes.basis: Voted for the millionaires' tax and campaigns on 'tax fairness for working families'; founding member of the Washington Tax Fairness Coalition.

housing.basis: Voted against the 2025 rent-increase cap, saying rent control 'has not stemmed the cost of housing,' while supporting more supply and affordable housing near transit.

safety.basis: Campaign site emphasizes community-led violence prevention and behavioral-health response services.

experience.basis: In the House since 1999 and chair of the Education Committee; the state's longest-serving House member.

local-control.basis: Opposes a universal school cellphone ban, preferring that local school boards decide.

immigration.basis: Founding board member of Hate Free Zone (OneAmerica) and an NCSL immigration task force; site cites protecting immigrant communities.

parental-rights.basis: As Education chair signed the do-pass report on HB 1296 and voted for final passage; the bill narrowed I-2081's curriculum, records and medical-notification rights.

candidates.summary: First-time candidate, Rainier Scholars leadership director and Seattle Planning Commissioner, running on generational change, rent stabilization and early education; won the primary.
highlights: Supports rent stabilization and says he would have voted for the 2025 rent-increase cap [S5][S7]
Priorities: housing affordability, childcare, interest limits on medical debt, early interventions for kids [S1]
Supports a statewide school cellphone ban [S5]
Endorsed by Gov. Bob Ferguson, Executive Girmay Zahilay, Superintendent Chris Reykdal, the WEA and The Seattle Times [S4][S6]

housing.basis: Prioritizes a real rent-stabilization cap and criticizes the incumbent's vote against the 2025 cap; anti-displacement focus.

spending.basis: Wants to fully fund early education and criticizes education cuts paired with forgone estate-tax revenue.

safety.basis: Campaign site calls for 'safety built on community investment,' including gun-violence prevention.

experience.basis: First-time candidate running explicitly on 'generation change' against a 27-year incumbent.

local-control.basis: Supports a statewide school cellphone ban, where the incumbent prefers local school-board discretion.

taxes.basis: Criticized the Legislature for giving up about $270M in estate-tax revenue while cutting education ('that doesn't make sense'). Endorsed by Tech 4 Taxes and Fuse Washington. He has no stated position on the millionaires' tax, so +1 rather than +2.

contests.office_does: One of two Washington State Representatives for the 41st District (Mercer Island, Newcastle and parts of Bellevue, Issaquah, Renton and Sammamish), voting on state law, budgets and taxes for two-year terms.
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Democrat Janice Zahn, appointed in 2025 and a former Bellevue councilmember, faces Republican Elle Nguyen, who opposes a state income tax and the 2026 state housing-siting mandate. Zahn took 72% in the August primary.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Representative since 2025 and former Bellevue councilmember (2017-2025); Port of Seattle chief engineer running on affordability, infrastructure investment and fiscal responsibility.
highlights: Voted for the 2026 tax on household income over $1 million (ESSB 6346), the tax I-645 would repeal [S8]
Voted for 2025 rent stabilization (EHB 1217) and the 2026 supportive-housing siting law (ESHB 2266) [S9][S10]
Says Washington must 'accelerate investments in clean energy and community resilience' to meet 2030 climate goals [S4]
Voted for ESHB 1296 (2025), the parents' rights amendments I-1 would undo; no public position found on the three initiatives [S7]

taxes.basis: Voted yea on ESSB 6346, the 9.9% tax on household income over $1 million; no further stated tax agenda.

spending.basis: Pairs 'delivering investments in housing, education, childcare, and transportation' with 'fiscal responsibility' and 'accountability' on budget challenges: genuinely mixed.

housing.basis: Voted for 2025 rent stabilization and for ESHB 2266 requiring cities to allow supportive housing and shelters.

climate.basis: Says the state must accelerate clean-energy investment to meet 2030 climate goals; endorsed by Conservation Action.

experience.basis: Sitting legislator since 2025 with eight prior years on the Bellevue council: an established record, though short legislative tenure.

local-control.basis: Voted for ESHB 2266, which requires cities to allow transitional and supportive housing and shelters in specified zones.

social.basis: Pamphlet endorsement list includes Planned Parenthood; no direct statement on gender or reproductive policy.

parental-rights.basis: Voted yea on ESHB 1296 (2025), which amended the I-2081 parents' rights law; single vote, no statement.

candidates.summary: Republican challenger from Mercer Island, a real estate investor and community advocate without prior elected office, running on fiscal discipline, public safety and local control.
highlights: Opposes a state income tax and says 'Olympia has been fiscally irresponsible' [S4]
'Adamantly opposes' ESHB 2266: 'Olympia should not substitute statewide mandates for the judgment of local communities' [S4]
Site lists 'Supporting law enforcement, holding criminals accountable' [S3]
States a commitment to 'parental rights' without specifics; no public position found on the three initiatives [S4]

taxes.basis: Opposes a state income tax and lists 'protecting taxpayers from unnecessary tax increases'.

spending.basis: Repeated calls for fiscal discipline, stopping wasteful spending and balancing the budget; says Olympia has been fiscally irresponsible.

safety.basis: Site lists supporting law enforcement and holding criminals accountable; no detailed enforcement agenda.

experience.basis: No elected office held; prior unsuccessful school-board and legislative runs.

local-control.basis: Adamantly opposes ESHB 2266 as a statewide mandate overriding 'the judgment of local communities'; commits to 'meaningful local control'.

parental-rights.basis: Repeatedly names 'parental rights' as a commitment, but no specific position on notification, curricula or opt-outs.

contests.office_does: One of two Washington State Representatives for the 43rd District (central Seattle), voting on state law, budgets and taxes for two-year terms.
contests.race_blurb: Two Democrats: Nicole Macri, in office since 2017 with a housing and homelessness record, faces first-time candidate Alby Clendennin, a UW resident director who emphasizes corporate influence in politics and AI regulation. Only Macri has stated positions on the statewide initiatives (no on all).

candidates.summary: Incumbent since 2017 and DESC deputy director; record centered on rent stabilization and supportive housing, with explicit positions on abortion access, gender-affirming care and the statewide initiatives.
highlights: 'I'm voting no on all statewide initiatives' (I-645, I-1, I-638) [S1]
Voted for 2025 rent stabilization and was an original sponsor of ESHB 2266, requiring cities to allow supportive housing and shelters [S8][S10]
Voted for the 2026 tax on household income over $1 million [S7]
Commits to 'fully funding access to abortion' and a 'sanctuary state for gender-affirming care' [S3]

taxes.basis: Voted for the millionaires tax and opposes I-645's repeal of it; also cites cutting small business taxes.

spending.basis: Cites tax revenue funding schools and childcare, funding supportive housing and fully funding abortion access.

housing.basis: Led on rent stabilization ('prevent rent gouging') and sponsored the supportive-housing siting law; DESC supportive-housing career.

climate.basis: 'Aggressively tackling climate change by modernizing our energy grid, cutting building emissions'.

experience.basis: Incumbent since 2017 with enacted housing legislation.

local-control.basis: Original sponsor of ESHB 2266, a state requirement that cities allow supportive housing and shelters in specified zones.

immigration.basis: Cites work to protect immigrant neighbors from 'hateful federal overreach'.

healthcare.basis: Frames healthcare as making care and insurance affordable and accessible within the current system; no single-payer statement.

social.basis: Explicit commitments to expand and fund abortion access and keep Washington a sanctuary for gender-affirming care; opposes I-638.

parental-rights.basis: Voted yea on ESHB 1296 (2025) and says she is voting no on all statewide initiatives, including I-1.

candidates.summary: First-time candidate and UW resident director who describes himself as a pragmatic progressive Democrat focused on reducing corporate influence in politics and regulating AI.
highlights: Priorities: 'reducing corporate influence in politics' and 'regulating artificial intelligence to prevent unfair pricing' [S1]
Calls for strengthening public services and 'a government that prioritizes people over profit' [S1]
No campaign website and no reported contributions as of mid-September 2026 [S1][S4]
No public position found on the three initiatives [S1]

experience.basis: No elected or government experience; first run for office.

reform.basis: Names reducing corporate influence in politics as a top priority; no specific reform proposals.

tech.basis: Wants to regulate AI to prevent unfair pricing.

contests.office_does: One of two Washington State Representatives for the 45th District (Kirkland, Redmond, Woodinville, Sammamish, Duvall), serving two-year terms writing state law and budgets.
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Democrat Roger Goodman, in the House since 2007 and chair of the Community Safety Committee, faces Republican JoAnn Tolentino, a retired music teacher and compliance professional making her first legislative run. Goodman took 72.87% in the August primary.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Representative since 2007 and chair of the House Community Safety Committee; attorney and former director of the state Sentencing Guidelines Commission.
highlights: Cites laws on crime survivors, drug and mental health services, and police accountability and training [S1]
Voted yes on ESSB 6346, the 2026 tax on household income over $1 million that I-645 would repeal [S6]
Voted yes on ESHB 1296, the 2025 parental-rights amendments that I-1 would undo [S5]
Pledges to champion K-12 funding, affordable housing investments, climate action and reproductive rights [S1]

experience.basis: House member since 2007 and chair of the Community Safety Committee, citing an enacted record.

taxes.basis: Voted for the 2026 millionaires' tax; his statement stresses tax relief for working people and small businesses rather than new revenue.

spending.basis: Cites free school meals and childcare funding and pledges K-12 and affordable-housing investment.

safety.basis: Record and platform center on police accountability reform and expanded drug and mental health services, alongside crime-survivor protections.

climate.basis: Pledges to champion climate action; primary-era campaign material cited carbon-cap legislation.

housing.basis: Pledges continued affordable-housing investments; no deregulation or rent-policy statement.

social.basis: Single explicit pledge to champion reproductive rights.

parental-rights.basis: Voted yes on ESHB 1296, which amended the I-2081 parents' rights law; no campaign statement on the topic.

immigration.basis: Campaign site criticizes 'masked ICE agents' who 'snatch people out of their vehicles and off the streets' and says this has eroded trust in local law enforcement: one clear statement toward constraining ICE tactics.

candidates.summary: Republican challenger from Woodinville, a retired music teacher and compliance-software professional and five-year precinct committee officer, running as "not a politician."
highlights: Says "parents, not politicians, should guide their children's education and healthcare" [S3]
Supports voter ID, paper ballots and bipartisan election oversight [S1][S3]
Would fight regulations driving up housing costs and streamline permitting and zoning [S1][S3]
Backs fossil fuels, nuclear and hydro to keep energy bills low [S3]

experience.basis: No public office beyond precinct committee officer; presents herself as "not a politician."

parental-rights.basis: Repeated statements: "empower parents"; parents "should guide their children's education and healthcare"; involve parents and reject CRT and gender-ideology content in classrooms.

local-control.basis: Calls to "restore local control" in schools, a single statement.

housing.basis: Would fight regulations driving up housing costs and streamline permitting and zoning to build more homes.

climate.basis: Champions affordable energy and supports fossil fuels, nuclear and hydro "to keep bills low."

safety.basis: "Full support for our law enforcement" paired with "treatment, not just punishment" and recovery programs.

spending.basis: "Audit every dollar and pass balanced budgets"; waste and fraud and fiscal accountability are recurring themes.

immigration.basis: Supports legal immigration, the rule of law and border security, with "humane processing."

contests.office_does: One of two Washington State Representatives for the 46th District in northeast Seattle, serving a two-year term writing state law and budgets.
contests.race_blurb: Two Democrats: seven-term incumbent Gerry Pollet, who led the primary with about 52%, and former federal prosecutor Will Dreher, who placed second with about 31% and has outraised him. AI regulation, housing and Pollet's long tenure frame the race.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Representative (in the House since 2011), chair of the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Committee, public-health faculty member and Hanford cleanup advocate.
highlights: Says he championed the millionaires' and capital gains taxes; voted yes on ESSB 6346 [S1][S11]
Calls himself 'a strong voice against the attacks on trans kids' and helped expand Medicaid coverage of gender-affirming care [S4]
Proposes taxing AI and data-center storage with Oregon legislators; says 10% annual rent increases are too high [S4][S9]
Voted yes on ESHB 1296 (2025), the parents' rights amendments that I-1 would undo [S10]

taxes.basis: Voted for ESSB 6346 and says he championed the millionaires' and capital gains taxes.

spending.basis: Frames new revenue as funding schools, healthcare, childcare and free college; his audit work targets tax breaks rather than spending restraint.

housing.basis: Backs density, but says 10% annual rent increases are too high and argues government must build housing for each income segment.

climate.basis: Says he worked to end fossil-fuel electricity and push life-cycle methane accounting; no stated carbon-pricing position.

experience.basis: In the House since 2011, JLARC chair and Appropriations member.

immigration.basis: Says he passed ICE mask bans and protected undocumented students from federal data sharing.

social.basis: Funded abortion access, opposes 'attacks on trans kids', helped expand Medicaid gender-affirming care coverage.

parental-rights.basis: Voted yes on ESHB 1296 (2025), which amended the I-2081 parents' rights law; no campaign statement on the topic.

tech.basis: Lists regulating AI and data centers and proposes an AI/data-center tax, with less emphasis than his opponent.

candidates.summary: Former federal prosecutor and Kagan clerk, now a plaintiffs' attorney, running his first campaign on aggressive AI and tech regulation.
highlights: Says he is 'the only candidate promising to aggressively regulate tech'; platform would regulate or stop new data centers [S1][S4]
Supports the No Hate in Washington State campaign 'to defeat Initiatives 1 and 638' [S4]
'I support the Millionaire's Income Tax, and I will fight any attempts to repeal it' [S4]
Pairs permitting reform and density with rent stabilization; proposes a North Seattle sex-trafficking task force [S4][S8]

taxes.basis: Supports the millionaires' income tax and pledges to fight repeal; proposes AI and corporate profits taxes.

spending.basis: Pamphlet plans to "fully fund schools"; platform adds aggressive transit investment, funded gun-violence reduction programs, a sex-trafficking task force, and emergency funding for LGBTQ+ newcomer organizations.

housing.basis: Permitting reform and density on one side, rent stabilization and supportive housing on the other.

safety.basis: Deterrence and a trafficking enforcement task force paired with non-police crisis response and evidence-based violence programs.

climate.basis: Would block diversion of Climate Commitment Act funds and stop or regulate new data centers to preserve climate progress.

experience.basis: First-time candidate with no elected or legislative experience.

immigration.basis: Would divest public funds from private detention facilities and provide healthcare regardless of immigration status.

social.basis: Supports defeating I-638 and emergency funding for LGBTQ+ newcomer organizations.

parental-rights.basis: Supports defeating I-1; his only parental-notification proposal concerns reading-assessment results.

tech.basis: Aggressive AI, data-center and social-media regulation is the centerpiece of his campaign.

contests.office_does: One of two Washington State Representatives for the 47th District (Kent, Auburn and Covington area of South King County), serving a two-year term writing state law and budgets.
contests.race_blurb: Eight-year Democratic incumbent Debra Entenman faces Libertarian housing developer Cobi Clark, who is endorsed by the 47th District Republicans. Clark would repeal the 2026 income tax and the 2025 parental-rights amendments; Entenman voted for both.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Representative since 2018 and former congressional district director. Running on her public safety funding and college student support bills and on the safety net.
highlights: Prime sponsor of HB 2015 (2025), which her pamphlet says secured $100 million for public safety [S1][S2]
Voted yes on ESSB 6346, the 2026 millionaires' tax that I-645 would repeal [S4]
Voted yes on ESHB 1296 (2025); her platform supports district-set curricula and comprehensive sex education, plus parental opt-outs from specific lessons [S3][S5]
Platform calls for independent investigations of police use of force and for social workers alongside officers [S3]
Endorsed by Washington Conservation Action, King County Democrats and The Urbanist [S9][S10][S11]

taxes.basis: Voted for the 2026 tax on household income over $1 million; no separate campaign statement on taxes.

spending.basis: Runs on strengthening safety-net programs (rental assistance, eviction prevention, childcare, healthcare) and investment in frontline responders.

housing.basis: Platform commits to rental assistance, eviction prevention and housing stability services.

safety.basis: Mixed: sponsored new public safety funding (HB 2015) while backing independent use-of-force investigations and social workers in safety response.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for ESHB 1296 and backs district-set curricula and comprehensive sex education, but her platform also supports parental opt-outs from specific lessons.

tech.basis: Platform calls for laws requiring companies to disclose and give consumers control over the personal data they collect.

experience.basis: In the seat since 2018, with four committee assignments and signed bills (HB 2015, HB 1559).

candidates.summary: Libertarian housing developer and construction project manager from Auburn, endorsed by the 47th District Republicans. Running on housing deregulation, opposition to the income tax, and civil liberties.
highlights: Would 'Repeal the state income tax contemplated under SB 6346' [S3]
Would 'Repeal HB 1296 which undermined the voter approved parents rights initiative 2081' [S3]
Would cut permitting delays and limit building codes to safety, based on his developer experience [S1][S7]
Would end qualified immunity, criminalize masked arrests, and ban Flock cameras [S3][S9]
Proposes multi-winner ranked-choice voting and advisory votes on new taxes [S4]

taxes.basis: Opposes any state income tax in the pamphlet and on his site, and would repeal the 2026 income tax in SB 6346.

spending.basis: 'Washington doesn't have a revenue problem. It has a spending problem'; would rein in spending, cut waste and tie spending to revenue sources.

housing.basis: Supply-side deregulation from developer experience: faster permits, building codes limited to safety, fewer regulations.

climate.basis: Puts affordable, 'abundant' energy and stopping 'policies that punish commuters' first, while also backing nuclear and geothermal investment; does not name carbon pricing.

parental-rights.basis: Would repeal ESHB 1296 to restore the I-2081 parental-rights law, and says schools should 'respect the role of parents in education decisions.'

reform.basis: Proposes multi-winner ranked-choice voting, restoring advisory votes on new taxes, and 50-year sunsets for legislation.

experience.basis: No elected office (lost a 2025 Auburn council race); runs on private-sector development experience.

contests.office_does: One of two Washington State Representatives for the 48th District (parts of Redmond, Bellevue and Kirkland plus the Points communities and Medina), serving two-year terms writing state law and budgets.
contests.race_blurb: Democrat Osman Salahuddin, appointed in 2025 and elected that November, faces Republican Jeffery Poppe, a retired CPA campaigning on no new taxes, fraud audits and individual-only contributions.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Representative appointed in January 2025 and elected in November 2025; former Redmond City Councilmember and Fred Hutch cancer researcher.
highlights: Passed 2025 bills on behavioral-health co-response teams and paid sick leave for immigration proceedings [S4]
Voted yes on ESSB 6346, the 2026 millionaires' tax that I-645 would repeal [S8]
Voted yes on ESHB 1296, the 2025 parental-rights amendments that I-1 would undo [S7]
Endorsed by Gov. Ferguson, the State Labor Council, teachers, nurses and Planned Parenthood Alliance [S1]

experience.basis: About two sessions in the House after a 2025 appointment and election, plus prior Redmond council service.

taxes.basis: Voted for the 2026 millionaires' tax and describes the 2025 budget's "equitable revenue measures."

safety.basis: Passed a co-response bill meant to "reduce reliance on law enforcement" and says safety means "prioritizing prevention"; also passed a sentencing aggravator for rape resulting in pregnancy.

immigration.basis: Sponsored the enacted paid-sick-leave law for immigration proceedings and cites immigrant-protection bills.

climate.basis: Calls for a just transition to clean energy with environmental justice in emissions reduction.

parental-rights.basis: Voted yes on ESHB 1296, which amended the I-2081 parents' rights law; no campaign statement on the topic.

candidates.summary: Republican challenger; retired CPA and financial systems consultant and former San Diego Taxpayers Association director, running on no new taxes and fraud audits.
highlights: "No more new taxes! Washington has an outrageous spending problem, not an income problem" [S1]
Pledges to spearhead fraud audits and publish spending and performance metrics [S1][S3]
Will accept only individual contributions, no PAC or union money [S1][S3]

experience.basis: No prior elected public office; runs on a private-sector auditing career.

taxes.basis: Repeated pledge to reject any new taxes; says the state has a spending problem, not an income problem.

spending.basis: Platform built on fraud audits, efficiency and spending transparency.

reform.basis: Repeated pledge to accept only individual contributions and refuse PAC and union money; no other structural-reform positions.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital, and transportation budgets, covering school funding, the tax structure, housing rules, behavioral-health funding, transportation projects, and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Appointed Democratic incumbent Zach Hall faces Republican Michelle Bennett, Mercer Island's police chief, after a close primary (44.5% to 43.0% in the King County count). The seat is on the ballot as both a short term and a full two-year term.

candidates.summary: Appointed in June 2025 and seeking election in his own right; Vice Chair of the House Environment & Energy Committee and a former Issaquah City Councilmember.
highlights: Voted for ESSB 6346, the 2026 tax on income over $1 million [S4]
Frames public safety around first responders, gun-violence prevention, and behavioral-health interventions [S2]
Commits to cutting greenhouse gas emissions and moving away from fossil fuels faster [S2]

taxes.basis: Recorded yea on House final passage of the 2026 tax on income over $1 million; no further public statement on revenue found.

spending.basis: Calls for more school funding, protecting essential services, and investment in infrastructure, childcare and healthcare access.

housing.basis: Housing platform centers on supply and reforms that make it easier to finance and build homes faster; no tenant-protection or social-housing position stated.

safety.basis: Describes safety as first-responder support, gun-violence prevention, and behavioral-health and substance-use interventions that meet people where they are.

climate.basis: Commits to reducing emissions and transitioning away from fossil fuels faster; endorsed by WA Conservation Action and Sierra Club.
